# The Honest Lies of Maps

Every map tells the truth, and every map lies. This is not a paradox but a simple fact of cartography: a map is a small, flat representation of a large, curved world, made for a specific purpose. Because of this, every map must simplify, distort, and choose. The question is never whether a map is accurate—it is whether it is honest about what it leaves out. A map can be perfectly accurate in its measurements and still lead a reader badly astray, because accuracy and completeness are not the same thing.

## The Problem of Scale

The first source of distortion is scale—the ratio between distances on the map and distances on the ground. This sounds impressively precise, but scale forces a brutal trade-off: the more terrain you cover, the less detail you can show, and vice versa.

# The Truth, the Whole Truth, and Nothing but the Truth: How Maps Mislead Without Lying

A map is a small model of a large world, and every act of shrinking the world requires choices. This is the central paradox of cartography: a map cannot lie outright without being useless, but it also cannot tell the whole truth, because the whole truth would simply be the landscape itself. What a map can do—and often does—is tell a partial truth so convincingly that we mistake it for the complete story. Understanding how this happens makes us better readers of maps and, more broadly, better consumers of all kinds of information.

## The Problem of Scale

Every map declares its scale, usually as a ratio: 1:24,000 means one inch on paper represents 24,000 inches in reality. This sounds precise and honest, and it is. But scale quietly determines what a map is *capable* of showing. Consider a hiking map of a mountain range at 1:50,000. At that scale, a trail three feet wide is far too small to draw to true proportion, so the cartographer exaggerates it into a visible line.
